title: Everolimus · neuroendocrine tumours
context_label: Progressive unresectable or metastatic pancreatic NET, or well-differentiated G1/G2 nonfunctional gastrointestinal NET under NCCP 00320b/c.
purpose: Everolimus is a daily targeted tablet used to help control particular advanced NETs. It aims to slow growth; the team balances disease control, side effects and your priorities. This NET guide does not cover the separate kidney-cancer indication.
schedule_summary: Take the prescribed everolimus dose once daily every day, at the same time and consistently with or without food. There is no planned tablet-free week.
scope_note: Progressive unresectable or metastatic pancreatic NET, or well-differentiated G1/G2 nonfunctional gastrointestinal NET under NCCP 00320b/c.
schedule_label: Daily treatment, with four-weekly safety blood tests
indication_text: Progressive unresectable or metastatic pancreatic NET, or well-differentiated G1/G2 nonfunctional gastrointestinal NET under NCCP 00320b/c.
phases_note: The written prescription and team review determine treatment; this timeline is a reference.
timeline_note: Treatment timing is shown for orientation. Symptoms can develop on any day; no symptom band predicts an individual toxicity peak.
safety_note: Follow your oncology unit’s emergency instructions. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice; do not wait for the next appointment. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or uncontrolled bleeding.
teachback: Can you explain the daily tablet plan, the four-week blood checks, mouth care and which breathing or infection symptoms need prompt contact?
consent_support: Discuss the exact NET indication, expected control and uncertainty, alternatives, mouth ulcers, infection and lung inflammation, metabolic and kidney/liver effects, interactions, pregnancy precautions and the monitoring plan.
urgent_extra: Contact oncology promptly for new or worsening cough, breathlessness or fever, mouth ulcers limiting eating or drinking, marked thirst, much less urine, severe diarrhoea or signs of infection. Severe breathing difficulty or collapse needs emergency help.

agents.name: Everolimus
agents.explanation: Everolimus blocks a growth-control pathway called mTOR inside cells. This can slow NET growth. Healthy tissues and immune responses also depend on these pathways, helping explain mouth ulcers, infections, lung inflammation and changes in blood sugar or fats.
agents.watch: Report mouth ulcers and new breathing symptoms early; keep blood and metabolic checks even if you feel well.
risks: Raised blood glucose and blood fats
Rash, diarrhoea, fatigue and reduced appetite
Impaired wound healing and radiation-related inflammation

passport_visit_note: Record the prescribed dose, doses taken or held, symptoms, blood tests and review dates. A stamp records care; it does not authorise the next dose.
anatomy: Mouth ulcers may appear early. Use prescribed mouth care; report soreness, pain or difficulty eating and drinking.
New cough, fever or breathlessness may be infection or lung inflammation. Contact oncology promptly; severe breathlessness is an emergency.
Blood counts can fall. Fever, shivering, unusual bruising or sudden illness needs urgent advice even without a scheduled visit.
Tests can change before symptoms occur. Attend blood checks and report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or persistent abdominal pain.
Kidney problems or protein in urine may need extra tests. Report swelling, dehydration or much less urine.
Diarrhoea, nausea or poor appetite can affect fluids and weight. Report persistent symptoms or inability to drink.
Rash and slow wound healing can occur. Report severe rash or unhealed wounds and discuss surgery before it is arranged.
Blood sugar and fats may rise without symptoms. Report marked thirst, frequent urine or unusual fatigue; keep the agreed tests.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects anchored to the full-body illustration. Blood, hormone and skin effects can involve more than one area. This is not a prediction or a complete side-effect list.
administration_text: The usual starting dose is 10 mg once daily, but follow your own prescription. Swallow whole with a glass of water; do not chew or crush. Take consistently with or without food. If a dose is missed, do not take an extra dose: take the next prescribed dose at the usual time.

phases.label: Daily everolimus
phases.detail: Continue daily only while the team confirms benefit and tolerability. Blood reviews do not create a planned tablet break.

timeline.label: Everolimus every day
timeline.text: Continue into the next review window unless your team tells you to hold.

timeline.label: Four-week safety review
timeline.text: Blood count, kidneys and liver; other checks on your individual plan.

day_groups.title: Starting safely
day_groups.body: Take the prescribed daily dose consistently with or without food. Start the mouth-care plan and check other medicines.
day_groups.action: Confirm the first blood-test date and who to call.

day_groups.title: Continue daily; report symptoms early
day_groups.body: Mouth, breathing, infection, bowel or skin symptoms can occur at any time. Do not wait for the four-week review.
day_groups.action: Attend blood checks and follow any written hold or dose-change instructions.

support.title: Mouth care
support.text: Use gentle mouth care and any prescribed alcohol-free mouthwash. Ask before buying a rinse; avoid products containing alcohol, peroxide, iodine or thyme. Report ulcers early.

support.title: Sickness and bowel support
support.text: Everolimus has minimal-to-low emetogenic potential. Routine premedication is not required by this regimen; agree any rescue anti-sickness or diarrhoea medicine with the team.

support.title: Infection prevention
support.text: Existing infection must be assessed and resolved before starting. Hepatitis B testing informs any specialist prevention plan. Vaccination and any antimicrobial prevention, including PJP prevention with certain steroid plans, are individual decisions.

support.title: Eating and energy
support.text: Report weight loss, poor intake or persistent fatigue. Ask for nutritional and symptom support; do not continue through severe symptoms simply to finish a pack.

monitoring_schedule.note: Your team books and reviews each test. Response scans and hormone or tumour markers follow an individual plan; they are not automatically required at every medicine review.

monitoring_summary: Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, BUN, urine protein, lipids, fasting glucose and hepatitis B screening. Blood count, kidney and liver tests every four weeks. Lipids regularly and glucose as clinically indicated; scans and NET markers follow the consultant plan.

chronology_notes.title: There is no planned rest week
chronology_notes.text: The 28-day visual is a review window. Do not take a routine week off or continue through a team-directed hold.

chronology_notes.title: Lung effects and infection can look similar
chronology_notes.text: A new cough or breathlessness needs assessment; do not assume it is a harmless tablet effect or start leftover antibiotics or steroids yourself.

chronology_notes.title: Monitoring continues after changes
chronology_notes.text: Ask who follows unresolved symptoms or abnormal tests after a delay, dose change or stopping.

sections.title: Taking tablets
sections.text: The usual starting dose is 10 mg once daily, but follow your own prescription. Swallow whole with a glass of water; do not chew or crush. Take consistently with or without food. If a dose is missed, do not take an extra dose: take the next prescribed dose at the usual time.

sections.title: Medicines, vaccines and food
sections.text: Avoid grapefruit and St John’s wort. Ask the pharmacist to check all prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal products. Live vaccines should be avoided during treatment; agree vaccination with your team.

sections.title: Procedures and radiotherapy
sections.text: Discuss planned surgery, wounds and current or recent radiotherapy. Everolimus may affect healing and can worsen or reactivate radiation-related inflammation. The teams agree any interruption.

sections.title: Safe storage and supply
sections.text: Keep tablets in their original labelled packaging, out of children’s reach, and follow the pack storage instructions. Return unused tablets to the pharmacy as advised. Plan repeat prescriptions before your supply runs out.

sections.title: Pregnancy, feeding and fertility
sections.text: Tell the team before starting if pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding. Ask for the medicine-specific contraception duration and fertility advice, and record it in your plan.

sections.title: Review visits
sections.text: Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, BUN, urine protein, lipids, fasting glucose and hepatitis B screening. Blood count, kidney and liver tests every four weeks. Lipids regularly and glucose as clinically indicated; scans and NET markers follow the consultant plan.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on the NET site and setting
evidence.intro: The principal trials assessed time before disease worsened.
evidence.population: RADIANT-3 studied advanced progressive pancreatic NETs; RADIANT-4 studied advanced progressive nonfunctional well-differentiated GI or lung NETs.
evidence.interpretation: Everolimus delayed progression compared with placebo in these trial populations. That does not mean cure or predict an individual response.
limitations: The studies do not provide one personal survival estimate. RADIANT-3 final overall survival did not show a statistically significant difference, with crossover complicating interpretation.
RADIANT-4 combined GI and lung populations; its inclusion of lung NET does not broaden NCCP 00320c.

chapters.title: Your everolimus treatment
chapters.intro: Daily treatment with regular safety reviews.

items.title: Why everolimus?
items.text: Everolimus is a daily targeted tablet used to help control particular advanced NETs. It aims to slow growth; the team balances disease control, side effects and your priorities. This NET guide does not cover the separate kidney-cancer indication.

items.title: The exact Irish NET indication
items.text: Progressive unresectable or metastatic pancreatic NET, or well-differentiated G1/G2 nonfunctional gastrointestinal NET under NCCP 00320b/c. The GI indication is nonfunctional; do not transfer it to lung NET or renal cell carcinoma.

items.title: How it works
items.text: Everolimus blocks a growth-control pathway called mTOR inside cells. This can slow NET growth. Healthy tissues and immune responses also depend on these pathways, helping explain mouth ulcers, infections, lung inflammation and changes in blood sugar or fats.

items.title: Trial evidence and limits
items.text: Everolimus delayed progression compared with placebo in these trial populations. That does not mean cure or predict an individual response. The studies do not provide one personal survival estimate. RADIANT-3 final overall survival did not show a statistically significant difference, with crossover complicating interpretation. RADIANT-4 combined GI and lung populations; its inclusion of lung NET does not broaden NCCP 00320c.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular NET
chapters.intro: Several different features help the team choose treatment.

items.title: Where it started and where it is now
items.text: A neuroendocrine tumour begins in cells with hormone-making features. Its starting organ and the places it has spread are separate parts of the diagnosis. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour differs from pancreatic adenocarcinoma; a deposit in the liver may have come from another organ.

items.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
items.text: The pathology report describes how organised the cells look (differentiation) and their growth activity (grade). Ki-67 measures cells showing a growth-related protein in the sample. Its percentage describes that sample, not the amount of your body affected or your chance of survival.

items.title: Grade is different from stage
items.text: Stage describes extent; grade describes tumour biology. Either can vary independently. A well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumour and a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are distinct diagnoses and may need different treatments.

items.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
items.text: A functioning tumour produces a hormone syndrome. A nonfunctioning tumour can still cause problems through growth or pressure. Somatostatin receptor uptake on a scan shows a treatment target; it does not, on its own, identify a hormone syndrome.

items.title: Your diagnosis record
items.text: Ask for one diagnosis summary: starting organ, grade, differentiation, Ki-67 result if reported, sites involved, hormone syndrome and receptor-imaging result. Keep pending results clearly marked.

chapters.title: Making sense of tests and results
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and hormone tests answer different questions.

items.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
items.text: Blood counts assess oxygen-carrying cells, infection-fighting cells and platelets. Kidney and liver results help assess treatment safety. These checks are needed even when you feel well; a reassuring scan answers a different question.

items.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
items.text: CT and MRI show anatomy and tumour size. Somatostatin receptor imaging tests whether a particular receptor target is present. An FDG-PET scan measures uptake of a glucose-like tracer and is used selectively. Your team chooses the scans that can guide your care.

items.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
items.text: Selected markers may help answer a hormone or tumour question. Examples include 5-HIAA for serotonin-related symptoms, chromogranin A, or a specific pancreatic hormone. They are not a routine panel for every neuroendocrine tumour. Interpret changes with symptoms and imaging.

items.title: Preparing for a test
items.text: Use the laboratory instructions for fasting, food restrictions and any timed urine collection. Some medicines affect marker results, including acid-suppressing medicines and chromogranin A. Ask the team what to do; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself.

items.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
items.text: Some hormone syndromes can affect heart valves, so an ultrasound of the heart may be requested. Inherited-risk assessment depends on the tumour and family history; multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is one example. An inherited-risk test and a test of tumour tissue answer different questions.

items.title: Who does what, and when?
items.text: For each test, write its name, purpose, booking date and result-review contact. Ask the team to set your next scan or marker date. A schedule for someone after surgery may not apply during your treatment.

chapters.title: Hormone symptoms and day-to-day changes
chapters.intro: A new symptom may come from the NET, treatment or another illness.

items.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
items.text: Keep a brief record of your usual bowel pattern, flushing, appetite, weight, pain and energy. Note new changes and when they started. This helps the team assess whether treatment, hormones or another problem needs attention.

items.title: Hormone-related symptoms
items.text: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.

items.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
items.text: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.

items.title: When a change is urgent
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency plan for sudden or severe symptoms. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency assessment. Severe diarrhoea, persistent vomiting, dehydration, fever or sudden illness needs urgent oncology advice. Do not wait for a scan, an online answer or the next clinic visit.

items.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
items.text: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.

chapters.title: Your overall plan and choices
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment plan.

items.title: What are we trying to achieve?
items.text: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.

items.title: How treatments fit together
items.text: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.

items.title: Choosing between options
items.text: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.

items.title: Evidence is about groups
items.text: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.

items.title: Review points and shared decisions
items.text: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.

chapters.title: Eating, energy, practical help and support
chapters.intro: Supportive care can be used alongside treatment from the start.

items.title: Food, weight and digestion
items.text: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.

items.title: Fluids and safe activity
items.text: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.

items.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
items.text: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.

items.title: Practical help
items.text: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.

items.title: A record that works without a phone
items.text: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.

items.title: Questions to take to the next visit
items.text: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.

questions.q: Which NET indication and treatment aim apply to me?
questions.a: Ask your team to name the exact pancreatic or nonfunctional GI NET indication, the treatment aim and how it fits with your previous care. This guide does not cover the separate kidney-cancer indication.

questions.q: When are my four-week blood tests and glucose/lipid checks?
questions.a: NCCP specifies blood count, kidney and liver tests every four weeks. Lipids are checked regularly and fasting glucose as clinically indicated. Write your actual test dates and result-review contact in the passport.

questions.q: What mouthwash or rescue medicines have you prescribed?
questions.a: Ask the team to write the mouth-care and any rescue medicine prescription. Alcohol-free mouthwash may be required; there is no automatic routine anti-sickness premedication in this regimen.

questions.q: What should I do about a new cough, fever or breathlessness?
questions.a: Contact oncology promptly. Infection and non-infectious lung inflammation can look similar and need assessment. Severe breathing difficulty or collapse needs emergency help.

questions.q: How does this fit with my hormone-control treatment?
questions.a: Ask the NET team to list any separate hormone-control medicine and its schedule. Do not stop injections or other prescribed treatment simply because everolimus is held.

questions.q: When will we review scans, symptoms and my priorities?
questions.a: The consultant sets the imaging and marker plan and reviews benefit, side effects and your goals. Ask for the next decision date and who will explain the results.

monitoring_test_details.label: 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only if requested for your hormone syndrome; the team sets the dates.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Measures a breakdown product of serotonin to help assess selected neuroendocrine tumours.
monitoring_test_details.detail: Often a timed urine collection. Follow the laboratory’s food and medicine instructions.

monitoring_test_details.label: Chromogranin A
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only when the team considers it informative for your tumour.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: A selected tumour-marker result, interpreted with symptoms and scans.
monitoring_test_details.detail: Acid-suppressing medicines and other conditions can alter the result. It is not a routine test before every treatment; do not stop medicines yourself.

monitoring_test_details.label: Selected pancreatic hormones
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only for the hormone question identified by your specialist.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Examples include gastrin, insulin or glucagon when the diagnosis or symptoms call for them.
monitoring_test_details.detail: The team names the test, preparation and review date; these are not a standard panel for every patient.
